common_name: Barr's Pink Aster (Semi-Double Clear Pink New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Barr's Pink is an English-raised New England aster selection valued for its clear, unfading pink color among mostly purple and rose-toned cultivars.

directions: Give this cultivar consistently moist, fertile soil and full sun, the same conditions that suit the wild New England aster. Barr's Pink carries semi-double, clear salmon-pink flowers with contrasting gold centers on sturdy, well-branched stems from late summer into fall, a distinct color break from the more common magenta and violet forms of the species. Its bushier, somewhat shorter growth reduces the need for staking compared with unimproved wild-collected plants, though pinching stems back by a third in early June still helps keep the clump compact. Divide every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and prevent the center of the clump from thinning out.

common_name: Hella Lacy Aster (Deep Violet-Purple New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Hella Lacy was selected and named by writer and plantsman Allen Lacy for its unusually vivid, deep royal-purple flower color.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, fertile soil in full sun for the strongest flower color and sturdiest stems. Hella Lacy produces an exceptionally heavy crop of deep violet-purple, gold-centered daisies over a tall, upright clump in early to mid fall, and it is widely regarded among native-plant growers as one of the richest-colored New England aster selections available. Because it can reach four feet or more, pinch the stems back once in late spring and again in early summer to encourage bushier, self-supporting growth and avoid the need for staking. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and airflow through the foliage.

common_name: Rudolf Goethe Aster (Large Lavender-Blue Italian Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; like other Italian aster selections, Rudolf Goethe resents heavy wet clay and prefers sharper drainage than most fall-blooming native asters.

directions: Site this long-cultivated European selection in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun rather than the rich, moisture-retentive ground favored by most border asters. Rudolf Goethe bears unusually large, clear lavender-blue daisies with bright yellow centers, opening from midsummer and well ahead of the New England and New York aster rush. The tidy, clump-forming habit does not run or self-seed aggressively, making it well suited to a small border, gravel garden, or rock garden edge. Lift and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the plant compact and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Brilliant is one of the older and more widely grown rose-pink selections of Italian aster in European perennial borders.

directions: Grow in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; heavy, poorly drained ground causes crown rot over winter. Brilliant produces abundant rich rose-pink, yellow-centered daisies on a compact, bushy plant that blooms earlier than most fall asters, typically beginning in late summer. The dense, non-spreading clump stays neat without staking and pairs well with ornamental grasses or other lean-soil perennials at the front of a border. Divide every two to three years in spring to keep clumps vigorous and free-flowering.

common_name: Wonder of Staffa Aster (Original Long-Blooming Lavender-Blue Frikart's Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Wonder of Staffa was among the earliest named selections from Swiss nurseryman Carl Ludwig Frikart's original amellus x thomsonii cross, predating the later Monch introduction.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun. Wonder of Staffa bears large, lavender-blue, orange-centered daisies over a long season stretching from midsummer into fall, on a somewhat looser and more open plant than the later Monch selection. It shares the exceptional bloom endurance that made the Frikart's asters famous among perennial growers, flowering steadily for months with only light deadheading. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and stake or lightly cage tall stems in windy or rich, fast-growing sites.

common_name: Flora's Delight Aster (Compact Pale Lavender Frikart's Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Flora's Delight is a dwarf, more compact Frikart's aster selection suited to smaller borders and front-of-bed placement than taller cultivars like Monch.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to encourage tight, low growth. Flora's Delight forms a low, spreading mound smothered in pale lilac-blue, yellow-centered daisies from midsummer well into autumn, offering the same long Frikart's aster bloom season in a scale suited to raised beds, rock gardens, or the front of a border. Its shorter stature means it rarely needs staking even in fertile soil. Divide every two to three years in spring to keep the clump from thinning at the center and to maintain dense, floriferous growth.

common_name: Jenny Aster (Dwarf Double Red-Purple New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jenny is one of the most widely sold dwarf Michaelmas daisies, commonly offered as fall-blooming garden center color.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Jenny forms a dense, mounded cushion covered almost completely in fully double, magenta-red flowers each autumn, one of the deepest colors available among compact New York aster selections. Its low, tidy habit suits container displays, edging, and small-space gardens where taller Michaelmas daisies would overwhelm the space. Divide every one to two years in spring, since dwarf novi-belgii selections tend to lose vigor and bloom quality faster than taller cultivars if left undivided.

common_name: Alert Aster (Dwarf Deep Red Michaelmas Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alert holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit as one of the deepest red dwarf Michaelmas daisies commonly grown.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest flower color and most compact growth. Alert produces a profusion of small, semi-double, deep crimson-red flowers over a very low, dense mound in early fall, standing out among the mostly blue, purple, and pink dwarf aster cultivars. Its tight habit makes it useful for edging paths or filling gaps at the front of a perennial border without staking. Divide every one to two years in early spring to keep the clump vigorous and prevent overcrowded centers from dying out.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Snowsprite is a dwarf white-flowered Michaelmas daisy selection used to brighten fall borders where most nearby asters bloom in shades of blue, pink, and purple.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Snowsprite forms a low, tight cushion of small, pure white, yellow-centered daisies that light up a fall border and combine easily with the deeper reds, pinks, and purples of other dwarf Michaelmas daisy cultivars. Its compact size and clean color make it a natural choice for container plantings and border edges where a bright, restrained accent is wanted. Divide every one to two years in spring to maintain a dense, floriferous habit and reduce the risk of powdery mildew in crowded plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Photograph is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection from the mid-twentieth-century era of British Michaelmas daisy breeding.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Photograph carries clear lavender-blue, semi-double flowers with a neat, even form over a medium-height, well-branched clump from late summer into fall, a reliable mid-border performer from the classic era of British aster breeding. It combines well with ornamental grasses and late-season perennials for a naturalistic fall display. Divide every two to three years in spring to renew vigor, and thin stems in late spring in humid climates to improve airflow and reduce powdery mildew.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Audrey is a compact dwarf Michaelmas daisy selection recommended by British growers for small borders and container displays.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Audrey produces masses of small, semi-double, mid-blue to lavender flowers over a low, dense, well-behaved mound in early autumn, staying tidy without staking. Its scale suits raised beds and the front of a border where taller Michaelmas daisies would crowd out neighboring plants. Divide every one to two years in early spring, since this dwarf type declines in vigor and flower count faster than taller novi-belgii cultivars if left undivided too long.

common_name: Crimson Brocade Aster (Semi-Double Deep Red New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Crimson Brocade descends from the twentieth-century Ballard breeding line of New York asters and is grown for its unusually deep red flower color.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Crimson Brocade bears semi-double, deep crimson-red flowers with gold centers on upright, well-branched stems from late summer into fall, offering one of the richest red tones among taller New York aster cultivars. Its medium height fits well in the middle of a mixed perennial border alongside ornamental grasses and other late bloomers. Divide every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, and stake in exposed sites if grown in rich soil that encourages lush, top-heavy growth.

common_name: Eventide Aster (Deep Violet-Purple Semi-Double Michaelmas Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Eventide is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection from the Ballard breeding line, valued for its large, deeply colored flowers on a sturdy, mildew-resistant plant.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Eventide produces large, semi-double, deep violet-purple flowers with gold centers on tall, sturdy stems from early to mid fall, holding up better against foliar disease than many older New York aster cultivars of similar height. Its strong upright habit works well toward the back of a border or as a backdrop for shorter dwarf asters. Divide every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, and space plants generously to promote airflow and further reduce powdery mildew pressure.

common_name: Coombe Fishacre Aster (Small Pink-Flushed Lilac Michaelmas Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Coombe Fishacre is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit cultivar named for the Devon garden where it originated, known for its two-toned flower color.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Coombe Fishacre produces abundant small, semi-double flowers that open pink-flushed and mature to soft lilac-blue, giving each cluster a subtle two-tone effect over a compact, well-branched clump in early fall. Its modest height and bushy form make it easy to place in the middle of a mixed border without staking. Divide every two to three years in spring to maintain flowering density and vigor.
